sec.s: Revision checklist

b.x: Database foundations begin with understanding the difference between data, information, a database, and the software that manages it. A DBMS provides structured ways to define, query, update, protect, and recover data. It can reduce common weaknesses of file-based approaches, especially when several users and applications share related information.

Data models describe the organization of data. The hierarchical model arranges records in a tree. The network model represents richer links among records. The relational model uses tables and keys and is widely used in business and application development.

The ER model helps designers describe a system before implementation. Entities represent the important things, attributes describe their properties, and relationships express how they are associated. Cardinality and participation capture important rules about how many entities can participate and whether participation is mandatory. An ER model can be mapped into relational tables using primary keys, foreign keys, and junction tables.
Integrity constraints help ensure that stored data follows defined rules:

x: PRIMARY KEY identifies rows uniquely and does not allow NULL.
FOREIGN KEY maintains valid references between related tables.
UNIQUE prevents duplicate values or combinations according to the DBMS's rules.
CHECK enforces a condition on values in a row.
NOT NULL requires a value to be present.

b.x: These constraints are essential, but they are only one part of reliable database engineering. Good design also requires understanding the real problem, choosing appropriate data types, modelling relationships accurately, avoiding unnecessary redundancy, using safe queries, controlling access, testing failure cases, and maintaining backups.

For practical learning, create a small database, define tables, insert valid data, deliberately try invalid values, inspect the errors, and query related tables with JOIN. This turns abstract concepts into observable behavior and builds the foundation for later work with APIs and backend applications.

sec.t: DBMS Architecture: Three-Schema Architecture and Data Independence
sec.s: Schemas, data independence, DBMS modules, users, languages and deployment tiers.

b.x: 13.1 Why study DBMS architecture?

Earlier topics explained what a DBMS does. This topic explains how a DBMS is organised inside, and how users at different levels see the same data in different ways. A good architecture lets many people share one database without everybody needing to know how the data is physically stored.
Two ideas run through the whole topic: separation of concerns (each layer does one job) and data independence (a change in one layer should not force changes in the layers above it).
13.2 The three-schema architecture (ANSI/SPARC)
The ANSI/SPARC architecture describes a database at three levels. Each level has its own schema, which is the description of the structure at that level.

x: External level
Many user views. Each view shows only the part of the database that a user group needs, for example a student view and an accounts-office view.
Conceptual level
One community view of the whole database: entities, attributes, relationships, constraints and data types. It hides storage details.
Internal level
The physical storage structure: files, pages, record formats, indexes, access paths and compression.
User A view    User B view    User C view     <- external schemas
|  Conceptual schema    |              <- logical design
|   Internal schema     |              <- files, indexes
Stored database

b.x: The DBMS keeps mappings between the levels. An external-conceptual mapping translates a query on a view into a query on base tables. A conceptual-internal mapping translates a request for a table into page reads on disk.
13.3 Data independence
Data independence is the ability to change the schema at one level without having to change the schema at the next higher level.

x: Physical data independence

You can change the internal schema, for example add an index, move a table to another disk or change the file organisation, without changing the conceptual schema or application programs. Queries stay the same; only their speed changes.
Logical data independence

You can change the conceptual schema, for example add a column or split a table, without rewriting existing external views or applications. This is harder to achieve fully, because applications often depend on the exact columns they use.

b.h: Example: a view protects an application
x: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Email, Phone, Fees_Paid, Address)
• The library application only needs RollNo and Name, so it uses a view.
• Later the college adds a column Blood_Group to STUDENT.
• The library view still returns RollNo and Name, so the library application does not change. This is logical data independence in action.
CREATE VIEW library_student AS
SELECT RollNo, Name FROM STUDENT;
-- External schema for the library; the base table can grow
ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Blood_Group TEXT;
SELECT * FROM library_student;   -- unchanged result shape
Physical independence is not 'no change at all'. Adding an index changes performance, not the meaning of queries. Do not mix this up with logical independence, which concerns the conceptual schema.

b.x: 13.4 Components of a DBMS
Most textbooks divide a DBMS into a query processor and a storage manager, supported by a transaction manager and a catalog.

x: DDL compiler
Reads CREATE, ALTER and DROP statements and records the schema in the catalog.
DML compiler and parser
Checks syntax, resolves table and column names using the catalog, and turns SQL into an internal form.
Query optimiser
Chooses an efficient execution plan, for example which index to use and in what order to join tables.
Execution engine
Runs the chosen plan, calling the storage manager for tuples.
Storage manager
Interfaces with the file system. It contains the file manager, the buffer manager and the index manager.
Buffer manager
Keeps frequently used disk pages in main memory and decides which page to evict when memory is full.
Transaction manager
Provides atomicity, isolation and durability using the lock manager and the recovery manager (log).
Catalog (data dictionary)
Stores metadata: table names, column types, keys, indexes, users and privileges. The catalog is itself stored as tables.
SQL text -> Parser -> Optimiser -> Execution engine
Transaction mgr  |  Buffer mgr
(locks, log)     |  (page cache)
v
File manager -> Disk
Every SQLite database has a table named sqlite_master (also called sqlite_schema) holding the CREATE statements. Try: SELECT name, type FROM sqlite_master; in the DBMS Lab.

b.x: 13.5 Database users and the DBA

x: Naive (end) users: use forms and mobile apps, such as a student checking marks.
Application programmers: write programs that embed SQL or call database APIs.
Sophisticated users and analysts: write SQL queries directly, often for reports.
Database designers: decide the schema, keys, constraints and views.
Database administrator (DBA): the person or team responsible for the running database.

b.x: Typical DBA duties are installation and upgrades, creating users and granting privileges, backup and recovery planning, performance tuning (indexes, statistics), monitoring disk space and locks, applying security patches and enforcing standards. In small projects one person plays all of these roles.
13.6 Database languages

x: DDL (Data Definition)
CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE. Defines structure.
DML (Data Manipulation)
SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. Reads and changes data. Some books place SELECT in a separate DQL group.
DCL (Data Control)
GRANT, REVOKE. Controls who may do what. Not available in SQLite, which has no user accounts.
TCL (Transaction Control)
BEGIN or START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.

b.x: DML can be procedural (the user says how to get the data) or declarative (the user says what is wanted). SQL is declarative; the optimiser decides how.
13.7 Application architectures: 1-tier, 2-tier, 3-tier

x: 1-tier
Application and database live together on one machine, for example a desktop program using SQLite. Simple, no network.
2-tier (client-server)
A client application talks directly to a database server using a driver such as JDBC or ODBC. Business logic is mostly on the client.
3-tier
Client (browser or app) -> application server (business logic) -> database server. The client never touches the database directly, which improves security and scalability.

b.x: In modern cloud deployments the database may be a managed service. The provider handles patching, backups and replicas, and 'serverless' databases scale capacity up and down automatically. The applications still connect through a driver or an API, so the logical design is the same.
13.8 Embedded database versus database server

x: Embedded (SQLite)
A library inside the application. The whole database is one file. No separate process, no user accounts, one writer at a time. Ideal for mobile apps, small tools and learning.
Server DBMS (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle)
A separate process serving many clients over a network, with user accounts, many concurrent writers, replication and fine-grained security.

A frequent 10-mark question: 'Explain the three-schema architecture with a diagram and define logical and physical data independence.' Draw the three levels, name the two mappings and give one example of each independence.

sec.t: The Relational Model Formally and Codd's Rules
sec.s: Domains, tuples, relations, keys, NULL semantics and Codd's twelve rules.

b.x: 14.1 Why a formal model?

The relational model, proposed by E. F. Codd in 1970, is based on set theory and predicate logic. Because it is formal, we can prove things about queries (for example that two queries are equivalent) and optimisers can safely rewrite them. Tables in SQL are an implementation of this model, with a few differences that we will note.
14.2 Basic terms

x: Domain
The set of permitted atomic values for an attribute, for example Age may take integers from 0 to 120.
Attribute
A named column that takes values from one domain.
Tuple
One row, an ordered list of values, one for each attribute.
Relation schema
The name of the relation and its attributes with domains, written R(A1, A2, ..., An). It changes rarely.
Relation instance (state)
The set of tuples present at a moment in time. It changes whenever data is inserted, updated or deleted.
Degree (arity)
The number of attributes in the schema.
Cardinality
The number of tuples in the instance.
Schema: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Age, Course)
Instance: {(1, 'Aarav', 19, 'BCA'), (2, 'Meera', 18, 'BCA'), (3, 'Kabir', 20, 'BBA')}
• Degree = 4 (four attributes)
• Cardinality = 3 (three tuples)
Cardinality of a relation means number of rows. 'Cardinality of a relationship' in ER diagrams (1:1, 1:N, M:N) is a different idea. Say which one you mean in the exam.

b.x: 14.3 Properties of a relation

x: Each relation has a distinct name and each attribute a distinct name within it.
Every attribute value is atomic (first normal form). Multivalued and composite values are not allowed inside one cell.
Tuples are unordered, because a relation is a set. The order in which rows are displayed has no meaning.
Attributes are unordered in theory, though SQL keeps the declared column order for convenience.
There are no duplicate tuples in the formal model, because a set cannot contain duplicates.

SQL tables are bags (multisets) unless a key or DISTINCT prevents duplicates. A table without a key can hold two identical rows, which the pure relational model does not allow. This is one reason to always declare a primary key.

b.x: 14.4 The key hierarchy
Keys are the heart of the model because they identify tuples and connect relations.

x: Superkey
Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies each tuple. {RollNo} and {RollNo, Name} are both superkeys.
Candidate key
A minimal superkey: no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness. {RollNo} and {Email} may both be candidate keys.
Primary key
The one candidate key chosen to identify tuples. It must be unique and NOT NULL.
Alternate key
A candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. Often declared UNIQUE.
Composite key
A key made of two or more attributes, for example (StudentID, CourseID) in ENROLMENT.
Surrogate key
An artificial identifier with no business meaning, such as an auto-generated number. It is stable and compact.
Foreign key
Attributes in one relation whose values must match a candidate key (usually the primary key) of another relation, or be NULL.
Primary key ⊆ Candidate keys ⊆ Superkeys

b.x: Counting rule: if a relation has n attributes and a single attribute A is a candidate key, then the number of superkeys is 2^(n-1), because every subset that contains A is a superkey.

x: R(A, B, C, D) with A as the only candidate key.
Superkeys are all subsets containing A: choose any subset of {B, C, D}.
Number of superkeys = 2^3 = 8.

b.x: 14.5 NULL: semantics and trouble

NULL is a marker meaning 'no value here'. It can mean unknown (a student's phone number exists but we do not know it), inapplicable (a spouse name for an unmarried person) or withheld. The model uses one marker for all of these, which is the source of confusion.

x: A comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN, not true or false. NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN.
WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is TRUE, so rows with UNKNOWN are dropped.
Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL to test for NULL.
Aggregates such as SUM, AVG and COUNT(column) ignore NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows.
Primary key attributes can never be NULL (entity integrity). Foreign keys may be NULL unless declared NOT NULL.
SELECT 1 WHERE NULL = NULL;        -- returns no rows
SELECT 1 WHERE NULL IS NULL;       -- returns 1
SELECT 5 + NULL;                   -- NULL
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, 'N/A');      -- N/A
NOT IN with a list or subquery that contains a NULL returns no rows at all, because x NOT IN (1, NULL) can never be TRUE. Prefer NOT EXISTS when NULLs are possible.

b.x: 14.6 Codd's rules
In 1985 Codd published twelve rules (numbered 1 to 12, plus a rule 0) as a yardstick for a true relational DBMS. They are often asked in exams.

x: Rule 0, foundation: a system must manage its database entirely through its relational capabilities.
Rule 1, information rule: all information is represented as values in tables.
Rule 2, guaranteed access: every value is reachable using table name, primary key value and column name.
Rule 3, systematic treatment of NULL: NULLs are supported uniformly and are different from empty strings and zero.
Rule 4, active online catalog: the catalog is stored as relations and queried with the same language.
Rule 5, comprehensive data sublanguage: at least one language supporting definition, manipulation, constraints, authorisation and transactions.
Rule 6, view updating: all theoretically updatable views must be updatable by the system.
Rule 7, high-level insert, update and delete: set-at-a-time operations, not only row-at-a-time.
Rule 8, physical data independence.
Rule 9, logical data independence.
Rule 10, integrity independence: integrity constraints are stored in the catalog, not in application code.
Rule 11, distribution independence: applications are unaffected by whether the data is distributed.
Rule 12, non-subversion: low-level access must not bypass the integrity rules.

No commercial DBMS satisfies all rules. For example, many views are not updatable (rule 6), SQL allows duplicate rows, and some systems allow row-by-row cursors that bypass set-oriented thinking. Codd's rules are best used as a checklist, not as a certification.
Group the rules: 1-4 about information and NULL, 5-7 about languages and views, 8-9 and 11 about independence, 10 and 12 about integrity. Writing the groups first helps you recall each rule.

sec.s: Specialization, generalization, inheritance, constraints, categories and aggregation.

b.x: 15.1 Why extend the ER model?

The basic ER model (Topic 4) handles entities, attributes and relationships. Real organisations also contain entities that are special kinds of other entities. A PERSON in a college may be a student, a teacher or both. Students have a roll number and a course; teachers have a salary and a department. Putting every attribute into one PERSON entity wastes space and creates many NULLs, while making separate unrelated entities loses the fact that both are people.
The Enhanced ER (EER) model adds the ideas of superclass and subclass, inheritance, specialization, generalization, categories and aggregation to deal with this.
15.2 Superclass, subclass and ISA

x: A superclass is a general entity type, for example PERSON.
A subclass is a more specific entity type that is a subset of the superclass, for example STUDENT and TEACHER.
The relationship between them is written ISA (is a): every STUDENT is a PERSON. In diagrams it is drawn as a triangle or a circle labelled d, o or with a U shape.
| PERSON |  (PersonID, Name, DOB)
(d)         <- disjoint specialization
| STUDENT | | TEACHER |
| Course  | | Salary  |

b.x: 15.3 Attribute and relationship inheritance

A subclass inherits all attributes of its superclass and also takes part in every relationship in which the superclass takes part. STUDENT automatically has PersonID, Name and DOB, and may add its own attributes such as Course. A subclass can also have its own relationships. For example only STUDENT participates in ENROLS_IN with COURSE.
Inheritance is the reason we do not repeat Name and DOB in every subclass. When the design is mapped to tables, the way inheritance is represented depends on the mapping option chosen in Topic 16.
15.4 Specialization and generalization

x: Specialization (top-down)

Start with a general entity type and define subclasses based on a distinguishing characteristic. Example: from EMPLOYEE define SECRETARY, ENGINEER and TECHNICIAN based on job type. This is called a specialization by job type.
Generalization (bottom-up)
Start with several entity types that share common attributes and combine them into a superclass. Example: CAR and TRUCK both have RegNo, Make and Year, so we generalise them to VEHICLE.

b.x: Generalization and specialization are the same structure viewed from opposite directions. The resulting diagram is identical; the difference is only how the designer arrived at it.
15.5 Constraints on specialization
Two independent constraints describe how subclasses relate to the superclass and to each other.

x: Disjoint (d)
An entity of the superclass can belong to at most one subclass. A PERSON is either a student or a teacher, never both.
Overlapping (o)
An entity can belong to more than one subclass at once. A PERSON can be both a student and a teacher (a research scholar who also teaches).
Total (double line)
Every entity of the superclass must belong to at least one subclass. Every VEHICLE must be a CAR or a TRUCK.
Partial (single line)
An entity of the superclass need not belong to any subclass. Some EMPLOYEEs are neither managers nor engineers.

b.x: Combining them gives four possibilities: disjoint-total, disjoint-partial, overlapping-total and overlapping-partial. Each must be stated in the ER diagram or in the design notes.

x: PERSON specialised into STUDENT and TEACHER. A research scholar can also take classes. Some people are visitors who are neither.
• Can a person be both? Yes, so the constraint is overlapping.
• Must every person be a student or teacher? No, visitors exist, so it is partial.
• Answer: overlapping, partial specialization.

b.x: 15.6 Predicate-defined and user-defined subclasses

x: Predicate-defined (condition-defined): membership is decided by a rule on an attribute. If EMPLOYEE has JobType, then SECRETARY is all employees with JobType = 'Secretary'. If one attribute decides the subclass, it is called an attribute-defined specialization.
User-defined: the database user decides membership by assigning each entity manually, for example which employees belong to a project committee.

b.x: 15.7 Categories (union types)

A subclass normally has one superclass. Sometimes an entity must be a subset of the union of different, unrelated superclasses. Suppose a vehicle can be registered by a PERSON, a COMPANY or a BANK. OWNER is a category (also called a union type) whose members are drawn from any one of those three.

x: OWNER ⊆ PERSON ∪ COMPANY ∪ BANK

b.x: An owner entity is a member of exactly one of the superclasses, unlike a shared subclass (multiple inheritance) where an entity inherits from all superclasses. Categories are mapped using a surrogate key because the superclasses have different primary keys.
15.8 Aggregation

Basic ER lets a relationship connect entities but not other relationships. Sometimes a relationship itself must take part in another relationship. Aggregation treats a relationship set, together with its participating entities, as one higher-level entity.

x: EMPLOYEE works-on PROJECT. The company also wants to record which MACHINE is used by an employee working on a project.
• The relationship works-on(EMPLOYEE, PROJECT) is aggregated into one abstract entity.
• A new relationship uses(that aggregate, MACHINE) is drawn.
• Without aggregation we would need a ternary relationship, which wrongly suggests that every machine use is a separate work assignment.

Aggregation is not the same as the part-of 'aggregation' in UML class diagrams or the aggregate functions of SQL. In ER modelling it means treating a relationship as an entity so that it can participate in another relationship.

b.x: 15.9 When to use EER

x: Use specialization when a group of entities has attributes or relationships that apply to only some of them.
Use generalization when several entity types share many attributes.
Do not specialise if the only difference is one optional attribute; a nullable column is simpler.
Keep hierarchies shallow. Deep hierarchies create many tables or joins when mapped.

Write the four labels: superclass, subclass, inheritance, and the pair (disjoint or overlapping, total or partial). A diagram with the correct d/o symbol and single or double line usually carries most of the marks.

sec.t: Mapping ER and EER Diagrams to Relational Schemas
sec.s: Step-by-step rules to turn a conceptual design into tables, with trade-offs.

b.x: 16.1 Why mapping is a separate step

An ER diagram is conceptual. A DBMS stores tables. Logical design converts the diagram into relation schemas by following a set of rules. Following the rules in order produces a schema that preserves the meaning of the diagram and avoids most redundancy.
16.2 Step 1: strong entity types
For each strong entity create a relation with all its simple attributes. For composite attributes include only the simple components. Choose one key attribute as the primary key.

x: STUDENT(RollNo PK, FirstName, LastName, DOB)
-- Name was composite (FirstName, LastName); Age is derived,
-- so it is not stored.

b.x: Derived attributes such as Age are computed from other data (DOB) and are usually not stored, to avoid inconsistency.
16.3 Step 2: weak entity types

A weak entity has no key of its own and depends on an owner entity. Create a relation with its simple attributes and add the primary key of the owner as a foreign key. The primary key of the new relation is the owner key plus the partial key of the weak entity.

x: DEPENDENT(EmpID FK, DepName, Relationship)
-- PK = (EmpID, DepName). EmpID references EMPLOYEE and is usually
-- ON DELETE CASCADE because a dependent cannot exist without them.

b.x: 16.4 Step 3: binary 1:1 relationships
Three options exist. Choose by looking at participation.

x: Foreign key approach
Put the primary key of one side as a foreign key in the other. Best choice is the side with total participation, to avoid NULLs. Example: DEPARTMENT and HEAD, add HeadID in DEPARTMENT.
Merged relation
Merge both entities into one table. Suitable when both have total participation and are almost always accessed together.
Cross-reference (relationship) relation
Make a third table with the two keys. Needed when participation is partial on both sides and few instances exist; it avoids many NULLs but adds a join.

b.x: 16.5 Step 4: binary 1:N relationships
Add the primary key of the 1 side (the parent) as a foreign key in the N side (the child). Any attributes of the relationship also move to the N side.

x: -- DEPARTMENT 1 ---- N STUDENT   (a student belongs to one department)
STUDENT(RollNo PK, Name, DeptID FK -> DEPARTMENT)

b.x: 16.6 Step 5: binary M:N relationships

Create a new relation (junction table, also called associative table) that holds the primary keys of both participating entities as foreign keys, plus any attributes of the relationship. The primary key is normally the combination of the two foreign keys.

x: -- STUDENT M ---- N COURSE with attribute Grade
ENROLMENT(RollNo FK, CourseID FK, Grade, PRIMARY KEY (RollNo, CourseID))

b.x: 16.7 Step 6: multivalued attributes

A multivalued attribute (such as PhoneNo for a student who may have several) cannot be a single column. Create a new relation containing the owner's key and the attribute. The primary key is the combination of both.

x: STUDENT_PHONE(RollNo FK, PhoneNo, PRIMARY KEY (RollNo, PhoneNo))

b.x: 16.8 Step 7: n-ary relationships

For a ternary relationship, such as SUPPLIER supplies PART to PROJECT, create one relation with the primary keys of all three entities as foreign keys plus relationship attributes (Quantity). The primary key is usually the combination of the keys on the N sides. Whether the primary key includes all three depends on the cardinality, so check which combinations must be unique.

x: SUPPLY(SupplierID FK, PartID FK, ProjectID FK, Quantity,
PRIMARY KEY (SupplierID, PartID, ProjectID))

b.x: 16.9 Step 8: mapping specialization and generalization
Consider PERSON(PersonID, Name, DOB) with subclasses STUDENT(Course) and TEACHER(Salary). There are four common options.

x: Option A: table per class (superclass + subclass tables)

PERSON(PersonID, Name, DOB), STUDENT(PersonID PK/FK, Course), TEACHER(PersonID PK/FK, Salary). Works for any constraint (disjoint, overlapping, total, partial). Needs a join to get all attributes of a student.
Option B: tables for subclasses only

STUDENT(PersonID, Name, DOB, Course), TEACHER(PersonID, Name, DOB, Salary). Works when specialization is total and disjoint. Querying all persons needs a UNION, and overlapping entities are stored twice.
Option C: one table with a type attribute
PERSON(PersonID, Name, DOB, PersonType, Course, Salary). Simple, no joins, but many NULLs, and it is best for disjoint specialization with few subclass attributes.
Option D: one table with Boolean flags
PERSON(PersonID, Name, DOB, IsStudent, Course, IsTeacher, Salary). Handles overlapping specialization with a flag per subclass, at the cost of NULLs.
Many subclass-specific attributes and mostly separate access: Option A. Total and disjoint with queries on subclasses only: Option B. Few subclass attributes and speed matters: Option C or D.

b.x: 16.10 Step 9: categories (union types)

For a category such as OWNER drawn from PERSON, COMPANY and BANK, create a relation for the category with a new surrogate key OwnerID, and add OwnerID as a foreign key in each superclass relation. This is needed because the superclasses have different primary keys.
16.11 A complete worked example

A college has DEPARTMENT, STUDENT, COURSE and ENROLMENT (with grade). A department offers many courses. A student belongs to one department and enrols in many courses. A student can have several phone numbers.

x: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;   -- SQLite needs this to enforce FKs
CREATE TABLE department (
dept_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
dept_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
CREATE TABLE student (
roll_no  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
name     TEXT NOT NULL,
dob      TEXT,
dept_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES department(dept_id)
CREATE TABLE student_phone (
roll_no  INTEGER REFERENCES student(roll_no) ON DELETE CASCADE,
phone_no TEXT,
PRIMARY KEY (roll_no, phone_no)
CREATE TABLE course (
course_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
title     TEXT NOT NULL,
credits   INTEGER CHECK (credits BETWEEN 1 AND 6),
dept_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES department(dept_id)
CREATE TABLE enrolment (
roll_no   INTEGER REFERENCES student(roll_no),
course_id INTEGER REFERENCES course(course_id),
grade     TEXT,
PRIMARY KEY (roll_no, course_id)

Forgetting to create a table for an M:N relationship; storing a multivalued attribute as a comma-separated string; putting the foreign key on the wrong side of a 1:N relationship (it always goes on the N side); and storing derived attributes.

Write the mapping rules in order: strong entities, weak entities, 1:1, 1:N, M:N, multivalued attributes, n-ary relationships, then specialization. Then apply them to the given diagram one rule at a time, showing the resulting schemas with underlined primary keys and marked foreign keys.

sec.t: Physical Storage, Buffer Management and File Organization
sec.s: Disks and pages, record layout, file organisations, buffer pool, RAID and I/O cost.

b.x: 17.1 Why physical storage matters

A table looks like a neat grid, but the DBMS must store it on a device. Main memory is fast but small and loses its contents when power is lost. Disks and SSDs are large and permanent but much slower. The central idea of physical database design is to reduce the number of disk accesses, because reading a page from storage costs far more time than processing it in memory.
17.2 Storage hierarchy

x: Registers and cache
Fastest, smallest, volatile. Managed by hardware.
Main memory (RAM)
Fast, volatile. Holds the buffer pool and working data.
Flash and SSD
Non-volatile, much faster random access than a spinning disk, but more costly per GB and with limited write endurance.
Magnetic disk (HDD)
Non-volatile, cheap, high capacity, slow for random access.
Tape and cloud archive
Very cheap and slow. Used for backups and archives.

b.x: 17.3 Disk blocks and access time
Data moves between disk and memory in fixed-size units called blocks or pages (commonly 4 KB to 16 KB, depending on the system). Even if you need one record, the whole page is read.
For a hard disk the time to access a block is the sum of three parts.

x: Access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time
Seek time: moving the read head to the right track.
Rotational latency: waiting for the right sector to rotate under the head, on average half a rotation.
Transfer time: reading the bytes once positioned.

b.x: Seek and rotation dominate for random access, which is why reading consecutive blocks (sequential access) is much faster than reading the same number of blocks scattered around the disk. SSDs have no moving parts, so they have no seek or rotational delay, and random reads are much faster than on HDDs. Sequential access is still usually the best pattern, and large databases still pay close attention to how many pages they touch.
17.4 Records and page layout

A record is stored as a sequence of bytes holding its field values. Records may be fixed-length (all fields of fixed size) or variable-length (for example VARCHAR or TEXT). Variable-length records are usually stored with a small header containing offsets or lengths.
Most systems use a slotted page layout for variable-length records.

x: | Page header (page id, #slots, free-space ptr) |
| Slot 0 | Slot 1 | Slot 2 | ...  ->               |
|             FREE SPACE                        |
|        <- ... Record 2 | Record 1 | Record 0   |

b.x: The slot directory grows from the start of the page and the records grow from the end. Each slot points to a record's offset. A record is identified by a record id (RID) made of page number and slot number. If a record moves inside the page, only its slot entry changes, so indexes that store the RID remain valid. Deleting a record frees its slot, and the page can be compacted later.
17.5 File organisations
A file is a collection of pages. The file organisation decides how records are placed in pages and therefore how fast different operations are.

x: Heap (unordered) file
Records are placed wherever there is space, usually at the end. Insert is fast. Finding a record without an index needs a full scan.
Sorted (sequential) file
Records are kept in order of a search key. Range queries and ordered scans are fast, and equality search can use binary search. Insert is costly because records must be kept in order.
Hashed file
A hash function on the key gives the bucket (page) number. Equality search is about one I/O. Range queries are not supported efficiently.
Clustered file
Records of related tables, such as a department and its students, are stored together to make joins cheaper.

b.x: 17.6 Cost model: counting page I/Os
A simple and exam-friendly model counts the number of page reads and writes. Let B be the number of pages in a file.

x: Full scan
Heap: B. Sorted: B. Hashed: about 1.25 B when buckets are around 80 percent full.
Equality search on the key
Heap: about B/2 on average if the record exists. Sorted: about log2 B. Hashed: about 1.
Range search
Heap: B. Sorted: log2 B plus the pages containing the answer. Hashed: B.
Insert
Heap: 2 (read the last page, write it). Sorted: search plus shifting records, up to about 2B in the worst case. Hashed: about 2.
A table has 100,000 records and 100 records fit in one page.
• Heap file, key equality search: about 1,000 / 2 = 500 I/Os on average.
• Sorted file, binary search: log2 1,000 is about 10 I/Os.
• Hashed file: about 1 I/O.
The numbers show why a good file organisation or an index can speed up searches by hundreds of times.

b.x: 17.7 Buffer pool and replacement policies

The buffer manager keeps a pool of page-sized frames in memory. When the DBMS needs a page, it asks the buffer manager. If the page is already in the pool (a buffer hit), no disk access is needed. If not (a miss), a page is read from disk into a free frame. If no frame is free, a victim page is chosen and, if it is dirty, written back first.

x: Pin count: a page in use by a query is pinned and cannot be evicted until released.
Dirty bit: set when a page has been modified. Dirty pages must be written to disk before the frame is reused.
Hit ratio: hits divided by total requests. A high hit ratio means fewer disk reads.
LRU (least recently used)
Evict the page not used for the longest time. Good for typical locality, but a large sequential scan can flush the whole pool.
MRU (most recently used)
Evict the most recently used page. Useful for certain repeated sequential scans larger than the pool.
Clock (second chance)

An approximation of LRU. Frames are arranged in a circle with a reference bit; the clock hand skips pages with the bit set (clearing it) and evicts the first page with the bit clear. Cheaper than exact LRU.
FIFO
Evict the oldest loaded page. Simple but ignores usage and can perform badly.

b.h: Why the DBMS does its own buffering
x: Operating systems also cache files, but a DBMS knows its access patterns and must control exactly when dirty pages reach disk for recovery (see crash recovery in Unit 3). This is why many DBMSs manage their own buffer pool.

b.x: 17.8 RAID
RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines several disks for speed, reliability or both.

x: RAID 0
Striping across disks, no redundancy. Fast, but failure of any one disk loses all data.
RAID 1
Mirroring: each block is written to two disks. Survives one disk failure. Usable capacity is half.
RAID 5
Striping with distributed parity. Survives one disk failure, needs at least three disks. Small writes are slower because parity must be updated.
RAID 6
Striping with two parity blocks. Survives two disk failures, needs at least four disks.
Striped mirrors. High speed and good reliability, at the cost of half the capacity. Common for busy database servers.
RAID is not a backup. It protects against disk hardware failure, but deleted or corrupted data is copied to every disk. Backups are still needed.

b.x: 17.9 Row store versus column store

x: Row store (NSM)
All fields of a record are stored together. Efficient for OLTP, where a transaction reads or writes whole rows, such as SQLite, MySQL and PostgreSQL by default.
Column store (DSM)
Each column is stored separately. Efficient for analytics that read a few columns across millions of rows, because only the needed columns are read and similar values compress well.

b.x: Example: SUM(fees) over 10 million students reads only the fees column in a column store, but every page of every row in a row store.

x: For a question on file organisation, draw a small comparison table of heap, sorted and hashed files against scan, equality search, range search and insert. Then state which one you would choose for a given workload.

sec.t: Indexing: B-Tree, B+ Tree and Hash Indexes
sec.s: How indexes speed up search, B+ tree insert and delete, hashing, and index design rules.

b.x: 18.1 What is an index?

An index is an additional data structure that lets the DBMS find rows by the value of one or more columns without scanning the whole table. It works like the index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page, you look up the word and go straight to the page numbers.
An index stores pairs of (search key value, pointer to the record). The search key is the column or columns that the index is built on. The table itself is called the data file.
18.2 Kinds of indexes

x: Primary index
Built on the ordering key of a sorted data file, one entry per page (sparse).
Clustering index
The data file is sorted on a non-key column, and the index has one entry per distinct value.
Secondary index
Built on a column that is not the ordering field. The index must be dense, with an entry for every record or distinct value. A table can have many secondary indexes but only one physical order.
Dense index
An index entry for every search key value in the data file.
Sparse index
Entries for only some search keys, for example one per page. Smaller, but needs the data file to be sorted on that key.

b.x: Many systems call the index that decides the physical order of rows a clustered index (for example InnoDB in MySQL uses the primary key as the clustered index). All other indexes are non-clustered or secondary, and they store the key plus a pointer such as a RID or the primary key of the row.

A multilevel index is an index on an index. If the first-level index is itself large, build a second-level sparse index over it, and so on, until the top level fits in one page. The B-tree family is the balanced, dynamic version of this idea.
18.3 B-tree and B+ tree

A B+ tree is a balanced, multiway search tree. Every path from the root to a leaf has the same length, and each node is a disk page, so a lookup takes one I/O per level. Nearly all relational systems use B+ trees as the default index type.

x: Fanout n: the maximum number of child pointers in an internal node. A node holds up to n-1 keys.
Internal nodes (except the root) have at least ceil(n/2) children.
Leaf nodes hold between ceil((n-1)/2) and n-1 keys with record pointers.
In a B+ tree, all record pointers are in the leaves. Internal nodes contain only keys used for routing.
Leaves are linked in key order, so a range scan finds the first key and then follows the links.
B-tree
Keys and record pointers can appear in internal nodes as well as in leaves. A key appears once. Search can end early. Fewer keys fit per internal node because pointers are stored there too.
B+ tree
Data pointers only in leaves, keys repeated in internal nodes for routing. Higher fanout, so a shorter tree, and linked leaves give fast range scans and ordered scans.

b.x: 18.4 B+ tree insertion with node split

Search for the leaf where the key belongs. If there is space, insert it. If the leaf overflows, split it into two and copy the smallest key of the new right leaf up into the parent. If the parent overflows, split it too (for internal nodes the middle key moves up rather than being copied).
Take fanout n = 4, so each node holds at most 3 keys. Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 25, 15 in that order.

x: Insert 40 overflows -> split into [10 20] and [30 40],
copy 30 up:                 [30]
Insert 25 -> leaf [10 20 25].
Insert 15 -> overflow [10 15 20 25] -> split, copy 20 up:

b.x: 18.5 B+ tree deletion

Search for the leaf and remove the key. If the leaf still has at least the minimum number of keys, stop. Otherwise first try to borrow a key from a sibling that has more than the minimum (and update the parent key). If no sibling can lend, merge the leaf with a sibling and remove the separating key from the parent, which may in turn underflow and be fixed in the same way.
With n = 4 the minimum is ceil(3/2) = 2 keys per leaf. Starting from the tree above, delete 25.

x: Leaf [20 25] becomes [20] -> underflow.
Siblings [10 15] and [30 40] have exactly 2 keys, so they cannot lend.

b.x: 18.6 Height and range queries

Because each node has many children, B+ trees are very shallow. With n children per node and K search-key values, the height is at most about log base ceil(n/2) of K. A tree with fanout in the hundreds can index millions of rows in only three or four levels, so a lookup needs three or four page reads, and the top levels are almost always in the buffer pool.
For a range query such as roll_no BETWEEN 200 AND 300, the DBMS descends to the leaf containing 200 and then follows the leaf links until it passes 300. A hash index cannot do this.
18.7 Hash indexes
A hash index applies a hash function h(key) to find the bucket holding the entry. It supports equality search in about one I/O but not ranges or ordering.

x: Static hashing
A fixed number of buckets. When many keys collide, overflow chains form and performance drops. Changing the number of buckets means rehashing everything.
Extendible hashing

A directory of bucket pointers indexed by the first d bits of the hash (global depth). Each bucket has a local depth. When a bucket overflows it splits, and the directory doubles only if needed. No overflow chains and no full rehash.
Linear hashing
Buckets are split one at a time in a fixed order, using a split pointer, without a directory. It grows smoothly as data grows.

b.x: 18.8 Other index types

x: Bitmap index: one bit vector per distinct value of a low-cardinality column, such as Gender or Status. Very compact and fast for combining conditions with AND and OR in analytics. Poor for columns with many distinct values or heavy concurrent updates.
Composite (multi-column) index: built on several columns such as (dept_id, name). It supports queries on the left-most prefix: dept_id alone, or dept_id and name together, but usually not name alone.
Covering index: contains all the columns a query needs, so the table need not be read at all.
Partial index: indexes only rows satisfying a condition, such as active students. Smaller and faster to maintain.
Expression index: indexes the result of an expression, such as lower(email), so that case-insensitive searches can use the index.
Unique index: enforces uniqueness. A UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint is normally implemented with one.

b.x: 18.9 The cost of indexes

x: Every INSERT, UPDATE of an indexed column and DELETE must also update each index on the table, so too many indexes slow writes.
Indexes occupy disk space and memory.
The optimiser may ignore an index if the query returns a large fraction of the table, because scanning is cheaper than many random lookups.
Indexes on very small tables bring no benefit.

b.h: When an index does not help
x: Wrapping the indexed column in a function (WHERE lower(name) = 'meera' with an index only on name), searching with a leading wildcard (LIKE '%ara'), or searching on the second column of a composite index without the first. Rewrite the query or create a matching index.

b.x: 18.10 Indexes in SQLite

x: CREATE TABLE student (
roll_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER, email TEXT);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM student WHERE dept_id = 3;
-- SCAN student           (no index: full scan)
CREATE INDEX idx_student_dept ON student(dept_id);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM student WHERE dept_id = 3;
-- SEARCH student USING INDEX idx_student_dept (dept_id=?)
CREATE INDEX idx_dept_name ON student(dept_id, name);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT dept_id, name FROM student WHERE dept_id = 3;
-- SEARCH ... USING COVERING INDEX idx_dept_name (dept_id=?)
CREATE INDEX idx_active ON student(email) WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_email ON student(lower(email));
DROP INDEX idx_active;

b.x: The exact wording of EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output varies between SQLite versions, but the words SCAN and SEARCH tell you whether an index was used. The DBMS Lab can be used to try these statements.

x: Definitions to memorise: dense versus sparse, clustered versus non-clustered, B-tree versus B+ tree. For insertion or deletion questions, always state the fanout, draw the tree after every step, and mention whether a key is copied up (leaf split) or moved up (internal split).

sec.t: Referential Actions, Data Types and Practical Constraint Design
sec.s: ON DELETE and ON UPDATE actions, deferrable constraints, choosing data types and keys.

b.x: 19.1 What happens to child rows?

A foreign key says that a child row must refer to an existing parent row. This raises a question: what should the DBMS do when someone deletes or changes a parent row that still has children? The answer is chosen by a referential action in the foreign key definition. Topic 5 introduced foreign keys; here we study the actions in detail.
19.2 The referential actions

x: NO ACTION
The statement fails if it would leave an orphan. The check is made at the end of the statement, which matters for deferred constraints. This is the default in most systems.
RESTRICT
Like NO ACTION, but the check is immediate and cannot be deferred. In some systems the two behave almost identically.
CASCADE
The change is propagated. Deleting the parent deletes all children; updating the parent key updates the children's foreign key values.
SET NULL
The foreign key column in the children becomes NULL. The column must be nullable.
SET DEFAULT
The foreign key column in the children is set to its DEFAULT value, which must itself be a valid parent key.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE department (dept_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE student (
roll_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
name    TEXT,
dept_id INTEGER REFERENCES department(dept_id)
ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE
INSERT INTO department VALUES (1, 'Computer Science');
INSERT INTO student VALUES (101, 'Aarav', 1), (102, 'Meera', 1);
UPDATE department SET dept_id = 10 WHERE dept_id = 1;
-- students now have dept_id = 10 (ON UPDATE CASCADE)
DELETE FROM department WHERE dept_id = 10;
-- students remain, dept_id = NULL (ON DELETE SET NULL)

b.x: 19.3 Choosing the right action

x: CASCADE for owned data: order items that belong to an order, phone numbers of a student, dependents of an employee.
RESTRICT or NO ACTION for important history: do not allow deleting a customer who has invoices.
SET NULL for optional links: a student's advisor leaves, the student remains.
Avoid long cascade chains that can delete far more data than the person expected. A single DELETE on a top-level table may remove thousands of rows.

SQLite parses foreign key clauses but does not enforce them unless you run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON for each connection. Without it, children can be orphaned and cascades will not happen, and no error is shown. Many students think their foreign keys work when they do not.

b.x: 19.4 Deferrable constraints

A constraint is normally checked after every statement. A deferrable constraint can be postponed until COMMIT. This is needed when two rows refer to each other, or when a transaction temporarily violates a rule while moving through several steps, for example swapping two unique values.

x: -- PostgreSQL / SQLite syntax
CREATE TABLE employee (
emp_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employee(emp_id)
DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO employee VALUES (1, 2);   -- manager 2 does not exist yet
INSERT INTO employee VALUES (2, 1);
COMMIT;                                -- check happens here, passes

b.x: Not every system supports deferrable foreign keys. MySQL with InnoDB does not support deferred constraints, so circular references are handled by inserting NULL first and updating later.
19.5 Choosing data types

A data type defines the permitted values, the storage size and the operations of a column. The right type is a form of integrity constraint, and a smaller type means more rows per page and faster scans.

x: Whole numbers
INTEGER (or SMALLINT, BIGINT in other systems). Use BIGINT when counts may pass about two billion.
Money

Never use floating point. FLOAT values such as 0.1 cannot be stored exactly, so totals drift. Use DECIMAL(p, s) or NUMERIC where available, or store the amount in the smallest unit (paise or cents) as an integer.
Text
Use VARCHAR(n) or TEXT as the system allows. Choose lengths from real needs, and never store numbers such as phone numbers or PIN codes as integers if leading zeros or symbols matter.
Boolean
BOOLEAN where supported. SQLite and MySQL store it as 0 and 1.
Dates and times
Use DATE, TIME and TIMESTAMP types where available. SQLite has no dedicated type and stores dates as TEXT (ISO-8601), REAL or INTEGER, so use the ISO form YYYY-MM-DD so that sorting works.
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3;           -- 0 (false) with floating point
SELECT (10 + 20) = 30;             -- 1 (true) using integer paise
-- store Rs 99.50 as 9950 paise

b.x: 19.6 Timestamps and time zones

x: Store moments in time in UTC and convert to the local time zone (such as IST, UTC+5:30) only when showing them to people.
Some systems offer a time zone aware type, for example TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE in PostgreSQL. Others store no zone information, so you need a convention.
Keep a created_at and updated_at column. Use the date type for things that are really dates, such as date of birth, which has no time zone.

b.x: 19.7 Natural versus surrogate keys, UUID versus sequence

x: Natural key
A real-world attribute such as an email, passport number or ISBN. Meaningful, but values can change, be reused, or turn out not to be unique.
Surrogate key
A generated number with no meaning. Stable and small, but you must also protect the natural identifier with a UNIQUE constraint.
Auto-increment or sequence
Small, ordered, index friendly. Easy to guess, so do not expose them as a security measure, and awkward when merging data from several databases.
UUID

A 128-bit identifier that can be generated anywhere without coordination. Good for distributed systems and merging. Larger than an integer, and random UUIDs scatter inserts across the index, which can slow writes. Time-ordered variants reduce this problem.
Use a surrogate primary key for stability, and put a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key. Both identify rows, but only the surrogate is used by foreign keys.

b.x: 19.8 Generated (computed) columns

A generated column is calculated from other columns of the same row. It avoids storing a redundant value that you must keep in sync by hand. It can be virtual (computed when read) or stored (computed when written). SQLite supports generated columns from version 3.31.

x: CREATE TABLE marks (
roll_no INTEGER, theory INTEGER, practical INTEGER,
total INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS (theory + practical) VIRTUAL

b.x: 20.1 Patterns and anti-patterns

After many years of building databases, designers have noticed solutions that work repeatedly (patterns) and mistakes that appear again and again (anti-patterns). Knowing both saves time and prevents hard-to-fix designs.
20.2 Pattern: audit columns

Add columns that record who created or changed a row and when. They help with debugging, accountability and support. Typical columns: created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by. A trigger or the application keeps them up to date. For full history, use a separate audit (history) table that stores old and new values.

x: CREATE TABLE student (
roll_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL,
created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
updated_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))

b.x: 20.3 Pattern: soft delete

Instead of removing a row, set a flag or a timestamp such as deleted_at. The row can be restored and old reports stay correct. The trade-offs: every query must filter out deleted rows, unique constraints must allow a deleted and a new row with the same value (use a partial unique index), and personal data may still need real deletion under privacy law.

x: ALTER TABLE student ADD COLUMN deleted_at TEXT;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_student_email ON student(email)
WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
CREATE VIEW active_student AS
SELECT * FROM student WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

b.x: 20.4 Pattern: junction table with its own attributes

An M:N relationship becomes a table (Topic 16). If the relationship has its own facts, such as the grade of a student in a course or the date a book was issued, they belong in that table. When the same pair can occur many times (a book issued to the same student twice), add a surrogate key or include the date in the primary key.
20.5 Modelling hierarchies
Categories, folders, organisation charts and comments with replies are hierarchies. SQL tables are flat, so there are several patterns.

x: Adjacency list
Each row stores its parent id. Simple and easy to update, but reading a whole subtree needs a recursive query (WITH RECURSIVE) or many round trips.
Materialized path
Each row stores its full path as text, such as /1/4/9/. A subtree is found with LIKE '/1/4/%'. Easy to read, but moving a subtree means rewriting many paths.
Closure table
A separate table stores every ancestor and descendant pair with the depth. Fast subtree and ancestor queries, and moves are possible, at the cost of extra rows.
Nested sets
Each node stores left and right numbers that bracket its descendants. Very fast to read, expensive to update.
CREATE TABLE category (
category_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
name TEXT NOT NULL,
parent_id INTEGER REFERENCES category(category_id)
-- all descendants of category 1 (needs SQLite 3.8.3+)
WITH RECURSIVE sub(id) AS (
SELECT category_id FROM category WHERE category_id = 1
UNION ALL
SELECT c.category_id FROM category c JOIN sub s ON c.parent_id = s.id
SELECT * FROM sub;

b.x: 20.6 Anti-pattern: entity-attribute-value (EAV)

EAV stores data in a table of (entity_id, attribute_name, value) triples to get a 'flexible' schema with no new columns. It looks attractive but causes trouble: no proper data types (everything is text), no NOT NULL or foreign key constraints, awkward queries that need one join per attribute, and poor performance. Alternatives are a normal table, a JSON column for truly free-form extras, or a document database if the data is really schema-less.

x: -- EAV (avoid for core data)
entity_id | attribute | value
101       | name      | Aarav
-- Retrieve one student as a row: pivot with many self-joins

b.x: 20.7 Anti-pattern: multiple values in one column

Storing a list in a single column, such as '98765,91234' in a phone field or 'DB,OS,CN' in a courses field, breaks first normal form. You cannot index or constrain individual items, searching needs LIKE, and updates are error-prone. Use a child table (Topic 16, multivalued attributes) instead.
20.8 Anti-pattern: polymorphic association

A single foreign key column that points to different tables depending on a second 'type' column, for example comment(target_id, target_type) where target_type is 'post' or 'photo', cannot be protected by a real foreign key. Better designs: a separate link table per target type, or a common supertype table (see EER mapping in Topic 16) that both post and photo reference.
20.9 Other common anti-patterns

x: Using FLOAT for money (Topic 19).
Missing primary keys, allowing duplicate rows.
Missing foreign keys 'for speed'. The cost is orphan rows that are very hard to clean up later.
Repeating column groups such as phone1, phone2, phone3.
One giant table for everything, with dozens of nullable columns.
Storing derived values that can go stale, for example total_marks maintained by hand.
Reserved words or spaces in names, and cryptic abbreviations.

b.x: 20.10 Temporal data: valid time and transaction time
Sometimes the history of data matters, not just its current value. Two different times can be tracked.

x: Valid time
When the fact was true in the real world. Example: a student's address was valid from 2023-06-01 to 2025-05-31.
Transaction time
When the database learned about the fact. Example: the address change was recorded on 2025-06-10.
Bitemporal table
Tracks both, so you can ask what we believed on a given date about a past period.
CREATE TABLE student_address (
roll_no INTEGER, address TEXT,
valid_from TEXT NOT NULL, valid_to TEXT,        -- NULL = current
recorded_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
PRIMARY KEY (roll_no, valid_from)

b.x: 20.11 Multi-tenant designs
A multi-tenant application serves many customers (tenants), such as many colleges using one software service. Three common patterns:

x: Database per tenant
Strong isolation and easy per-tenant backup, but high operating cost with many tenants.
Schema per tenant
One database, one schema each. Medium isolation and cost.
Shared tables with tenant_id

All tenants in the same tables, every table has tenant_id and every query filters by it. Cheapest and scales well, but a missing filter leaks data. Row-level security can enforce the filter inside the database.

b.x: 20.12 Naming conventions and the data dictionary

x: Choose one style, for example snake_case, and use it everywhere.
Use singular or plural table names consistently (student or students, not both).
Name primary keys clearly (student_id) and foreign keys the same as the key they reference.
Avoid prefixes like tbl_ and avoid reserved words.

b.x: A data dictionary documents every table and column: its meaning, type, allowed values, owner and example. It is the human-readable partner of the catalog. Keeping it with the schema in version control helps new team members, auditors and report writers.

x: If asked for 'good database design practices', answer in four groups: keys and constraints, correct data types, normalisation with deliberate exceptions, and naming and documentation. Then give two anti-patterns with their fixes.

b.x: 21.1 Worked example: a view as an external schema
Question: the college stores full student records, but the notice-board application must see only roll number, name and department. Show how an external schema gives logical data independence.

x: -- conceptual schema (one table for the whole college)
CREATE TABLE student (roll INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT,
dept TEXT, cgpa REAL, city TEXT);
INSERT INTO student VALUES (1,'Asha','CSE',8.6,'Patna'),
(2,'Ravi','ECE',7.2,'Ranchi'),
(3,'Meera','CSE',9.1,'Gaya');
-- external schema for the notice board
CREATE VIEW v_public AS SELECT roll, name, dept FROM student;
SELECT * FROM v_public WHERE dept = 'CSE';
-- roll | name  | dept
--    1 | Asha  | CSE
--    3 | Meera | CSE

b.x: The application never mentions cgpa or city, so it cannot read them. If the DBA later adds a column (for example email) to student, the view and every program that uses it keep working unchanged. That is logical data independence: the conceptual schema changed, the external schema did not. If the DBA moves the table to a different disk or builds an index, only the internal schema changed and even the view definition is untouched: physical data independence.

x: Always name the three levels in your answer: external (view), conceptual (table definitions), internal (files and indexes). Then say which level changed and which did not.

b.x: 21.2 Worked example: ER diagram to relational schema

Problem: Publisher publishes many books (1:N). Book has ISBN, title and a multivalued attribute author. A Copy is a weak entity identified by (ISBN, copy number) and has a shelf. A Member borrows copies; each loan records an issue date and a due date (M:N relationship with attributes).

x: PUBLISHER and MEMBER are strong entities: one table each, key becomes primary key.
BOOK is strong: one table. The 1:N relationship Publishes puts the foreign key pub_id on the N side (BOOK).
The multivalued attribute author gets its own table BOOK_AUTHOR(isbn, author) with a composite primary key.
COPY is weak: its table takes the owner's key (isbn) plus the partial key (copy_no) as its primary key; the foreign key to BOOK uses ON DELETE CASCADE because a copy cannot exist without its book.

The M:N relationship Borrows becomes the table LOAN. Its key combines the keys of both sides plus issue_date, so the same member can borrow the same copy again later; issue_date and due_date are attributes of the relationship.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE publisher (pub_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, pub_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE book (isbn TEXT PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL,
pub_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES publisher(pub_id));
CREATE TABLE book_author (isbn TEXT REFERENCES book(isbn) ON DELETE CASCADE,
author TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (isbn, author));
CREATE TABLE copy (isbn TEXT REFERENCES book(isbn) ON DELETE CASCADE,
copy_no INTEGER, shelf TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (isbn, copy_no));
CREATE TABLE member (member_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE loan (member_id INTEGER REFERENCES member(member_id),
isbn TEXT, copy_no INTEGER, issue_date TEXT NOT NULL, due_date TEXT NOT NULL,
PRIMARY KEY (member_id, isbn, copy_no, issue_date),
FOREIGN KEY (isbn, copy_no) REFERENCES copy(isbn, copy_no));
Putting the foreign key on the wrong side of a 1:N relationship, or forgetting the extra key column (issue_date) in LOAN. Without it a member could never borrow the same copy twice.

b.x: 21.3 Worked example: height of a B+ tree and page I/Os
Given: block size 4096 bytes, key 8 bytes, pointer 8 bytes, table with 10,000,000 rows of 100 bytes each, an index on the primary key.

x: Step 1: maximum pointers per node p, from (p - 1) x 8 + p x 8 <= 4096
Step 2: leaf nodes needed (full leaves): ceil(10,000,000 / 255) = 39,216
Step 3: next level up: ceil(39,216 / 256) = 154 internal nodes
Step 4: next level up: ceil(154 / 256) = 1 node = the root
Height = 3 levels (root, one internal level, leaves)
Exact-match lookup = 3 index pages + 1 data page = 4 page I/Os
Table scan: rows per page = floor(4096 / 100) = 40
Speed-up of the index for one row: 250,000 / 4 = 62,500 times fewer I/Os

b.x: In practice nodes are 50 to 100 percent full (about 69 percent on average after random inserts), so real fanout is smaller, but the height stays 3 or 4. That is why even a billion-row table needs only a handful of page reads per lookup.

x: Repeat the calculation with 4-byte keys and 4-byte pointers: p = 512, the height is still 3 for 10 million rows. Smaller keys mean more entries per page, which is why short integer keys make better indexes than long strings.

b.x: 21.4 Worked example: B+ tree insertion with splits (max 3 keys per node)
Insert the keys 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50 in this order into an empty B+ tree where every node holds at most 3 keys.

x: 5, 10, 15 fit in one leaf: [5 10 15].
Insert 20: the leaf overflows, so it splits into [5 10] and [15 20]. The smallest key of the new right leaf (15) is copied up into a new root [15].
Insert 25: goes to [15 20 25]. Insert 30: overflow, split into [15 20] and [25 30]; copy 25 up. The root is now [15 25].
Insert 35: [25 30 35]. Insert 40: overflow, split into [25 30] and [35 40]; copy 35 up. The root is [15 25 35] (full).

Insert 45: [35 40 45]. Insert 50: overflow, split into [35 40] and [45 50]; copy 45 up. The root would become [15 25 35 45], which overflows, so the internal node splits: keys 15 and 25 stay left, 45 stays right, and the middle key 35 moves up (it is moved, not copied, for internal nodes) to form a new root.

b.x: The tree grew in height only when the root split, so all leaves are always at the same depth. A range query such as keys 20 to 40 finds 20 through the tree and then follows the leaf chain: [15 20] -> [25 30] -> [35 40].

x: At a leaf split the middle key is COPIED up (it stays in the leaf); at an internal split it is MOVED up. Mixing these rules up is the most common error in B+ tree questions.

b.x: 21.5 Worked example: choosing indexes for three queries
Tables: student(roll PRIMARY KEY, name, dept, cgpa, city) and enrol(roll, course, grade). Queries:

x: Q1: SELECT * FROM student WHERE dept = 'CSE' AND cgpa > 8;
Q2: SELECT * FROM student WHERE city = 'Patna';
Q3: SELECT s.name, e.course FROM student s JOIN enrol e ON e.roll = s.roll WHERE e.course = 'DBMS';
-- before any extra index (SQLite EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN):
Q1: SCAN student
Q2: SCAN student
Q3: SCAN e  +  SEARCH s USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)
CREATE INDEX idx_dept_cgpa   ON student(dept, cgpa);
CREATE INDEX idx_enrol_course ON enrol(course);
-- after:
Q1: SEARCH student USING INDEX idx_dept_cgpa (dept=? AND cgpa>?)
Q3: SEARCH e USING INDEX idx_enrol_course (course=?)
+ SEARCH s USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)
Q1 uses a composite index: equality column first (dept), range column second (cgpa), following the left-most prefix rule.
Q3 needs an index on the filter column enrol.course; the join into student already uses its primary key.
Q2 is run rarely and city has few distinct values per page of data, so we decide NOT to index it: every index slows inserts and updates and uses space.
A query on cgpa alone would still scan, because cgpa is not the left-most column of idx_dept_cgpa.
A good answer to an index-selection question lists, for each query, the filter columns, the order of columns in a composite index, and one reason to leave some column unindexed.

b.x: 22.1 Three-schema architecture

x: External level
Many user views. Shows each user group only what it needs. Implemented with views and privileges.
Conceptual level
One community view of the whole database: tables, constraints, relationships. Hides storage details.
Internal level
Physical storage: files, pages, indexes, compression. Chosen by the DBMS and DBA for performance.

b.x: 22.2 Data independence

x: Logical data independence
Change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas or programs. Harder to achieve; needs view mappings.
Physical data independence
Change the internal schema (indexes, file organisation) without changing the conceptual schema. Easier and widely achieved.

b.x: 22.3 Codd's rules at a glance

x: Rule 0
System must manage the database entirely through relational capabilities.
Rule 1 Information
All information is represented as values in tables.
Rule 2 Guaranteed access
Every value is reachable by table name, primary key value and column name.
Rule 3 NULLs
Missing information is represented systematically, independent of data type.
Rule 4 Catalog
The online catalog is itself relational and queried with the same language.
Rule 5 Sublanguage
At least one language supports DDL, DML, integrity rules, authorisation and transactions.
Rule 6 View updating
All theoretically updatable views are updatable by the system.
Rule 7 Set-level operations
Insert, update and delete work on sets of rows, not only one row.
Rule 8 Physical independence
Programs are unaffected by storage changes.
Rule 9 Logical independence
Programs are unaffected by logical schema changes when possible.
Rule 10 Integrity independence
Integrity constraints are stored in the catalog, not in programs.
Rule 11 Distribution independence
Programs are unaffected by whether data is distributed.
Rule 12 Non-subversion
Low-level access cannot bypass integrity rules.

b.x: 22.4 EER constraints

x: Disjoint (d)
An entity can belong to at most one subclass.
Overlapping (o)
An entity can belong to several subclasses at once.
Total (double line)
Every superclass entity must belong to some subclass.
Partial (single line)
A superclass entity may belong to no subclass.
Category (union)
A subclass whose members come from different superclasses; an entity belongs to only one of them.

b.x: 22.5 ER to relational mapping rules

x: Strong entity
Table with its attributes; key becomes primary key.
Weak entity
Table with owner's key plus partial key as primary key; foreign key to owner.
Foreign key on either side (prefer the total-participation side) or merge the tables.
Foreign key on the N side.
M:N
New junction table; primary key combines both foreign keys; relationship attributes go here.
Multivalued attribute
New table (owner key, value).
Ternary relationship
New table with the three foreign keys.
Specialization
One table, table per subclass, or table per concrete class, chosen by the constraints and queries.

b.x: 22.6 File organisations

x: Heap
Fast insert; full scan for search. Good for bulk loads.
Sorted
Binary search on the key and fast range queries; costly inserts.
Hashed
About one I/O for equality search; useless for ranges.

b.x: 22.7 RAID levels

x: RAID 0
Striping only. Fastest, no redundancy; one disk loss loses everything.
RAID 1
Mirroring. Survives one failure per mirror pair; half the capacity.
RAID 5
Striping with distributed parity. Survives one disk failure; slow small writes.
RAID 6
Two parity blocks. Survives two failures.
RAID 10
Mirrored stripes. High speed and good safety; half the capacity.

b.x: 22.8 Index types

x: Clustered / primary
Data rows are stored in index order; at most one per table.
Secondary
Separate structure pointing to rows; many per table.
Dense / sparse
Dense has an entry for every key; sparse has one per block and needs sorted data.
B+ tree
Balanced, height about 3 to 4, supports equality and range, leaves are linked.
Hash
Equality only, no range, no ordering.
Bitmap
Good for low-cardinality columns in read-mostly analytics.
Composite
Several columns; usable only from the left-most prefix.
Covering
Contains every column the query needs, so the table is never touched.

b.x: 22.9 ON DELETE actions

x: NO ACTION / RESTRICT
Reject the delete if children exist.
CASCADE
Delete the children too.
SET NULL
Set child foreign key to NULL.
SET DEFAULT
Set child foreign key to its default value.

b.x: 22.10 Design anti-patterns

x: EAV
Generic (entity, attribute, value) rows: no types, no constraints, painful queries.
Comma-separated list in a column
Breaks 1NF; cannot join or enforce foreign keys; use a junction table.
Polymorphic association
One foreign key column pointing at several tables: no referential integrity.
Float for money
Rounding errors; use integer paise or DECIMAL.
Missing keys or indexes on foreign keys

b.x: 23.1 Questions with answers

x: 1. Explain the three-schema architecture and why it is useful.

It separates the database into external, conceptual and internal levels. External schemas give each user group a tailored view, the conceptual schema describes the whole database logically, and the internal schema describes storage. The separation gives data independence, so storage or logical changes do not force every program to be rewritten.
2. Differentiate logical and physical data independence with an example of each.

Physical independence means the internal schema can change (for example, adding an index or moving files) without changing the conceptual schema or applications. Logical independence means the conceptual schema can change (for example, adding a column) without breaking external views or programs. Logical independence is harder because view mappings must be updated.
3. What are the main components of a DBMS?

The query processor (parser, optimizer, executor), the storage manager (file manager, buffer manager, index manager), the transaction manager (concurrency control and recovery) and the catalog or data dictionary. Together they translate a query into plans, fetch pages, keep transactions ACID and store metadata.
4. Distinguish DDL, DML, DCL and TCL with one command each.

DDL defines structure (CREATE TABLE). DML manipulates and queries data (INSERT, SELECT). DCL controls privileges (GRANT). TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK). SELECT is sometimes classed separately as DQL.
5. State any six of Codd's rules and comment on how real systems comply.

For example Rule 1 (information rule), Rule 2 (guaranteed access), Rule 3 (systematic NULL treatment), Rule 4 (relational catalog), Rule 6 (view updating) and Rule 8 (physical independence). Real systems follow most of them but not fully; Rule 6 in particular is only partly met because many views are not safely updatable.
6. Why is NULL problematic in the relational model?

NULL can mean unknown, not applicable or missing, and the model cannot tell which. It introduces three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN), so NULL = NULL is not true, aggregates skip NULLs and NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows. Designers reduce trouble with NOT NULL constraints and careful modelling.
7. What is the difference between specialization and generalization in the EER model?

Specialization is a top-down process that defines subclasses of a superclass based on distinguishing characteristics (PERSON into STUDENT and TEACHER). Generalization is bottom-up: common attributes of several entity types are factored out into a superclass. Both produce the same ISA structure.
8. Explain disjoint/overlapping and total/partial constraints.

Disjoint means an entity can be in at most one subclass; overlapping means it can be in several. Total means every superclass entity must be in at least one subclass; partial means it may be in none. The two pairs combine independently, giving four possibilities.
9. How is a 1:N relationship mapped to tables?

Place the primary key of the 1 side as a foreign key in the table of the N side, along with any attributes of the relationship. No new table is needed. The M:N case differs: it needs a junction table.
10. Why does a weak entity table include the owner's key in its primary key?

A weak entity has only a partial key, which is unique just within one owner. Combining the owner's key with the partial key identifies each weak entity globally, and the owner's key also acts as the foreign key linking it to its owner.
11. Compare heap, sorted and hashed file organisations.

A heap file inserts quickly but searching needs a scan. A sorted file supports binary search and range queries but inserts are costly. A hashed file finds a key in about one I/O but cannot answer range queries. The best choice depends on the workload.
12. Why is a B+ tree preferred over a binary tree for database indexes?

Disk access is by pages, so a node should fill a page. A B+ tree has a very high fanout (hundreds of children), keeping the height at about 3 or 4 even for millions of rows, and it stays balanced under inserts and deletes. Linked leaves make range scans efficient.
13. A composite index on (dept, cgpa) exists. Which of these queries can use it: WHERE dept='CSE'; WHERE cgpa>8; WHERE dept='CSE' AND cgpa>8?

The first and third can use it, because they use the left-most prefix. The second cannot use it efficiently because cgpa is not the left-most column, so the optimizer will normally scan the table or use another index.
14. Give two anti-patterns in database design and their fixes.

Storing several values in one comma-separated column breaks 1NF; use a junction table with one row per value. Entity-attribute-value tables lose types and constraints; use proper columns, or a JSON column for truly sparse data.

b.x: Three-schema architecture
External, conceptual and internal levels. They give logical and physical data independence.
DBA
The person or team responsible for schema design, security, backup, tuning and monitoring.
Relation schema vs instance
The schema is the table definition; the instance is the set of rows at a moment in time.
Degree and cardinality
Degree is the number of attributes of a relation; cardinality is the number of tuples.
Specialization and generalization
Top-down creation of subclasses versus bottom-up factoring of a superclass.
Junction table
The table that implements an M:N relationship; its primary key combines the two foreign keys.
Page and buffer pool
The page is the unit of disk transfer; the buffer pool caches pages in memory with a replacement policy such as LRU or clock.
B+ tree
A balanced multiway tree storing all keys in linked leaves; the standard index structure of relational systems.
Clustered index
An index whose order matches the physical order of rows; only one per table.
Covering index
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table is not accessed.
Referential action
The rule (CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT and so on) that decides what happens to child rows when a parent row changes.
Anti-pattern
A common design that looks convenient but causes recurring problems, such as EAV or comma-separated lists.
